1.1: 1.1 The Parables of Solomon. It is to be noted that the Vulgate edition says parables, which in Hebrew is mishle, in Greek paroimiai, that is, proverbs; but it fits well enough. For parables, because they are hidden, are so named, and are rightly called proverbs also: because they are such as often ought to be on the lips of speakers and held in memory. Proverbs also are for the most part so obscure that they are well called parables; whence: These things I have spoken to you in proverbs, John 6., etc. The book of Proverbs does not, as the simple suppose, have plain precepts, but as gold in the earth, a kernel in a nut, fruit hidden in the shaggy husks of chestnuts is sought, so in them the divine sense must be sought more deeply. The Parables of Solomon, translated from the Hebrew truth by Eusebius Jerome the priest, at the request of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus; in Greek, in Latin similitudes; which word Solomon therefore put on this work, that we may not understand according to the letter what he says: in which he signifies the Lord about to speak in parables to the crowds, as also by his own name, the peaceful kingdom, the kingdom of Christ and of the Church; of which: His empire shall be multiplied, and of his kingdom there shall be no end. He shall sit upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, Luke 1. As by the building and dedication of the temple, the building of the Church in the time of the resurrection. Christ himself also the son of David, and spiritual king of Israel, according to the testimony of the crowd that met him with palm branches and praises, Matthew 21. What usefulness they have is shown in the title, when it is said: To know wisdom and instruction; that is, how one ought rightly to believe and live, and where each is to direct the intention of his heart.
1.2: 1.2 To understand the words of prudence. That is, that they not only embrace the wisdom which they have received, and serve the discipline of virtues, but also hearken to and skillfully understand the words of prudence by which they may advance.
1.5: 1.5 A wise man hearing shall be wiser. Beautifully he begins from wisdom, because, the choice being given him, he asked wisdom and received it. A wise man hearing shall be wiser. He shows that no one is so wise in this life that he cannot be wiser even by the sayings of his inferiors. The queen of Sheba, a lesser, heard Solomon, the greater, and returned wiser. Moses heard his father-in-law, much inferior, and was made wiser. And he that understands. RABANUS in Proverbs, tome 5. Let no one boast of his knowledge, etc., down to to know wisdom and instruction, etc.

7.26: 7.26 And the strongest have been slain by her. As Solomon himself, the wisest, etc., down to who denies it errs.
7.27: 7.27 Her house is the way to hell, reaching. But of the Church the Lord says: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it, Matthew 16. The inner chambers of death. The darker and straiter torments of Gehenna, in which it is certain that heretics and fornicators are to be plunged.
8.1: 8.1 Does not wisdom, etc. The Lord spoke openly to the world: and in secret he said nothing. Why then, neglecting his Gospel, do the wretched flock to heresy and wantonness?
8.2: 8.2 On the top, etc. On the mountain he taught the disciples and the crowds together, etc., down to who speak in secret against him?
8.4: 8.4 O men, to you. He cries to men, that is, to strenuous hearers of the word: for in either sex women, that is, flowing minds, cannot take in the words of wisdom.
8.5: 8.5 Understand, little ones, etc. It is manifest of the Lord, etc., down to he seeks those whom he may be able to seduce.
8.7: 8.7 My lips. The two testaments, etc., down to opened throughout the whole world to preach salvation.
8.13: 8.13 Arrogance. Arrogance and pride in them, etc., down to but according to the pleasure of the hearers they change their words.
8.14: 8.14 Mine is counsel. Let not human presumption exalt itself: the fullness of virtues the wisdom of God alone possesses, from it human weakness receives whatever virtue it has.
8.15: 8.15 By me kings. He calls the apostles kings, etc., down to for he says: Without me you can do nothing, John 15.
8.17: 8.17 I love those who love me, etc. He who loves me shall be loved by the Father: and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him, John 14. Early indeed they watch for wisdom, who with renewed zeal of mind strive to attain to the vision of Christ.
8.18: 8.18 With me are riches. Proud riches, lofty riches he says, etc., down to and we await his promises, in which is justice.
8.22: 8.22 The Lord possessed me. Hitherto he has spoken in parable to the Son, but now, because he had made mention of wisdom and had not said what it was, and of how great dignity, he as it were incidentally shows and commends it according to both natures, namely the divine and the human, the Lord says, etc. The ways of the Lord are the works, etc., down to for his flesh is on account of the works, his divinity before the works.
8.31: 8.31 Playing in the world. Because when times and the creatures of the world began, he himself, what he was, the Son, was abiding in the Father: this, that none might forbid him to be with creatures and times.
8.34: 8.34 At my gates. The Scriptures, or the teachers; the same are also the doorposts, without which we cannot enter into the life he promises.
9.1: 9.1 Wisdom has built. Because he had said sufficiently about the eternity of the divinity of Christ, etc., down to because he raised up those separated from love of the world to bear the fabric of the Church. Seven pillars. Namely the Churches throughout the world, etc., down to as if by sustaining they held it together.
9.5: 9.5 Come, eat my bread. The divinity and humanity joined in the one person of Christ, or, in the bread his body, in the wine his blood, with which we are filled at the altar.
9.6: 9.6 Forsake. After the banquet offered he adds also admonitions of life, that those whom he refreshes with the received mysteries of his incarnation he may likewise instruct with words of doctrine.
9.7: 9.7 He that teaches, etc. As if you should ask, etc., down to and believing him greater.
9.8: 9.8 Rebuke not. There is no need to fear, etc., down to but for the grace of his love to cease.
9.12: 9.12 If you be wise. I admonish you to wisdom, which however profits you, not me. For if you are wise, etc.
9.13: 9.13 A foolish woman. Above he commended wisdom through divinity and humanity, now by contrast he shows the same more commendable, where the foolish woman, etc., who is contrary to her, sits, etc. A woman, etc. The woman here is heresy, etc., down to this is lifted up in the pride of the mind.
9.16: 9.16 Whoso is a little one. Wisdom the little ones and the foolish, etc., down to and to turn aside to herself.
9.17: 9.17 Stolen waters. Wisdom openly set the table for all, etc., down to she asserts that forbidden and unlawful unions are sweeter.
9.18: 9.18 And he knew not that there. The adulterous woman knows not, etc., down to and the guests of the faithful in the heights of heaven.
10.1: 10.1 The Parables of Solomon. He sets a new title, because a new kind of speech begins, namely that he no longer, as before, discourses long on the single parts of the good or of the wicked; but by alternate verses describes the acts of both. A wise son. He who well keeps the mysteries of the faith received gladdens God the Father; he who defiles them by evil action or heresy saddens the mother, the Church.
10.2: 10.2 Treasures of wickedness shall profit nothing. And from transitory death, etc., down to which they confer because they were given for life.
10.3: 10.3 The Lord will not afflict. And if at any time, etc., down to by just vengeance turns back.
10.4: 10.4 Poverty is wrought. He who lives negligently in this world will want goods in the future; but those who valiantly fight for the Lord are rewarded with the riches of eternal beatitude.
10.5: 10.5 He that gathers. He who gathers to Christ the souls of the faithful is a wise son. And indeed the harvest is great but the laborers few, Matthew 9. But he who in this acceptable time is sluggish in caring for his salvation shall be confounded in the day of tribulation.
10.6: 10.6 But the mouth of the wicked. The mouth that served revelry, drunkenness and evil conversations will be condemned for the iniquity it heaped up. Finally iniquity covered the mouth of him who, placed in torments, sought refreshment for his tongue, in which for many crimes he was more punished.
10.7: 10.7 The memory. In this life the good by the good, etc., down to and their fire shall not be quenched.
10.8: 10.8 The fool is beaten with lips, either his own, by which he deserved to be condemned, because death and life are in the hands of the tongue, Isaiah 66., or of those by whom, because he could not be corrected, he received the sentence of damnation; whence: Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips, Psalm 119.
10.9: 10.9 He that walks, who knows how to live simply, etc., down to and receives what is worthy of his deeds, for nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed, Matthew 10.
10.13: 10.13 A rod on the back. Vengeance in the life that follows, etc., down to rightly is added: The wise hide, etc.
10.15: 10.15 The substance of the rich. Spiritually: He who is rich toward God by good works trusts in him, as one in an impregnable city that no enemy can overcome; but those who are straitened by lack of virtues, therefore lack heavenly riches, because with harmful fear they dread to bear hard labors for the Lord.
10.18: 10.18 They hide knowledge, etc. If therefore you desire to be truthful and wise, neither conceal hatred in the hidden heart nor bring it forth through insult of the mouth; but let your heart be filled with love and your mouth with truth.
10.23: 10.23 A fool works wickedness as it were for sport. Prudence took its name from foreseeing. He is therefore a fool who rejoices in wickedness. It is the part of the wise, and of him who is worthy of the name of man, to foresee that laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and the joys of sinning will be followed by the punishment of vengeance.
10.24: 10.24 What the wicked fears shall come upon him. He speaks of that wicked man, etc., down to what they hold in the heart will come.
10.25: 10.25 As a tempest. He speaks of the persecutors of the Church, who seek to overturn the house of faith. But she, placed on the true foundation, that is in Christ, they themselves at once perish.
10.26: 10.26 As vinegar to the teeth. As the perfidy of heretics, etc., down to and also assail with words, whence: They went out from us, but they were not of us, 1 John 2.
10.28: 10.28 But the hope. Not against what is said above, etc., down to Of those who sin knowingly, he adds.
10.29: 10.29 The strength of the simple is his way, and fear. If the obscure things of the Scriptures, etc., down to they scorn to do.
11.1: 11.1 A deceitful balance. Either of money or of judgment, etc., down to and agrees with the action.
11.2: 11.2 Where pride is. The proud either behave insolently through contempt or through ignorance of discipline, or heap insult on their neighbors, or he who exalts himself shall be humbled.
11.7: 11.7 When the wicked man is dead. This Origen did not know, etc., down to and perhaps what follows pertains to them. The expectation of the careful. The care of the good is to fulfill the precepts of God; but of the wicked who sin knowingly, that they will be snatched to eternal punishment. And therefore the expectation of the former will be crowned; of the latter condemned, even before the judgment, their own conscience condemning.
11.9: 11.9 The hypocrite. The heretic feigning Catholic doctrine deceives his hearer. Those who follow the truth of the Gospel will be delivered by Catholic wisdom, lest they be taken in the heretical snare.
11.12: 11.12 He that despises, etc. He is not to be despised who loves us simply, even if he acts ineptly: for he who does this lacks wisdom. But the prudent man is silent in public, corrects in secret, which is better opened in what follows.
11.14: 11.14 Where there is no governor, the people shall fall, but in much counsel there is safety. Lest you should think, etc., down to that he may be corrected by many.
11.15: 11.15 He shall be afflicted. According to the letter it is plain, etc., down to renders himself worthy of vengeance before the eyes of the strict judge. But he that avoids snares shall be secure. He will be secure in the future who now is rightly fearful and cures his sins by penance, and keeps himself free from the company of the impenitent.
11.21: 11.21 Hand in hand. He who joins hand in hand, etc., down to whence was said before: The perverse heart is abominable to the Lord.
11.22: 11.22 A golden ring in a swine's nose, etc. If you fix a ring of gold in your nostrils, etc., down to because given to carnal things.
11.27: 11.27 He rises early who seeks good things, etc., that is he rises to life in the time of the resurrection, because now he does good in the time of working. But he who seeks evils to say or do is held back from higher things by their weight.
11.28: 11.28 But the just shall spring up like, etc. As those who do good in the present from hope of future rewards justly receive what they hope. For a green leaf on a tree signifies the fruit not yet shown to be coming: and the just spring up like a green leaf, who, saved by hope, cease not to advance in the grace of faith and virtues.
11.29: 11.29 He that is a fool. The wicked lives for the pious; the one is condemned, the other receives the prize for which he strove.
11.30: 11.30 He that takes. He who for the Lord takes up the care of souls, etc., down to he provides that he may reign more loftily with the Lord.
11.31: 11.31 If the just man. If the martyrs suffer so much unjustly, etc., down to for though we are not impious, certainly if we deny that we are sinners, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
12.1: 12.1 He that is good, etc. The connection of these verses is this; he who is good does not trust in his own thoughts; but seeks the grace of the Lord, and through it lives piously. But he who trusts in his own thoughts cannot be good: for he who cares not to seek the grace of God continues in evil action.
12.4: 12.4 A woman. According to the letter, a good and chaste woman, etc., down to the rot of perverse doctrine corrupts.
12.5: 12.5 The thoughts. The just their deeds, etc., down to forgetful of the fear of the Lord.
12.7: 12.7 Overthrow the wicked. Much impiety in the gods of the Gentiles, etc., down to but whatever members arrive here and there find the joys they hoped for.
12.10: 12.10 Knows, that is sympathizes with the dullness and frailty of the neighbors committed to him. But the bowels of the wicked are cruel, who do not sympathize with subjects; but as the Lord says: They strike the boys and handmaids, saying: My lord delays to come.
12.12: 12.12 The desire. The wicked desires, etc., down to he says on the contrary of the good. But the root of the just shall prosper, faith, hope, charity, in which they are rooted in Christ do not deceive them; but they will receive more than they hope in the future.
12.16: 12.16 A fool, etc. He who desires to avenge in the present is a fool; but he who for the Lord despises is wise. But he who dissembles: does not so wish it hidden that it last, but that it be wholly blotted out; for it is the nature of anger that spoken it burns the more; hidden, it languishes.
12.18: 12.18 But the tongue of the wise is health, etc., because the good things they promise they themselves by fulfilling attain to life; and to others they show what follows.
12.19: 12.19 The lip of truth, etc. The Catholic faith will always remain; but he who suddenly inserts new dogmas is a minister of falsehood.
12.23: 12.23 A crafty man. Wise and prudent: who at times conceals knowledge, either not able to speak as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal; or unwilling to give the holy to dogs, or to cast pearls before swine, or to send. The heart of fools provokes. Either when they desire to know more than it behooves to know, and vanishing in their thoughts, have and hold folly for wisdom; or pressing on others things they cannot take in, as the light of the sun to weak eyes, that is of the wisdom which they seemed to have, they take away.
12.24: 12.24 The hand of the strong. The perfect not only overcome the wars of vices, but also rule over the chosen brethren by greater grace of virtues. But what is slack. Those dissolute in mind, etc., down to for we must not despair of such, when he adds, the sorrow of the just, etc.
12.25: 12.25 Sorrow in the heart, etc., because it is needful that first the sorrow of penance humble the sinner wholesomely, and afterward the word of reconciliation given by the judgment of the priest gladden or refresh him. He who neglects loss, etc. If this is taken literally, etc., down to or hands over the flesh itself to death?
12.27: 12.27 He shall not find, etc. For money acquired by fraud, etc., down to by which the brightness of eternal life is bought, more precious than gold.
13.1: 13.1 A wise son. So great is the distance between the wise and the fool, that the one sometimes by progress in learning comes to teach him who had taught him: the other, when rebuked, will not hear.
13.4: 13.4 The sluggard wills and wills not. He wills to reign with the Lord, etc., down to and Jesus son of Sirach: Woe to the sinner entering the land by two ways. But the soul of those who do the Lord's commands shall be made fat, because it will be refreshed with the sweetness of the things above; whence: As with fat, Psalm 26., etc.; or, those who sweat in pious labors for the Lord will be given an unfading crown.
13.7: 13.7 There is one who seems rich, not truly, like him who was clothed in purple and fine linen, Luke 16.; but because he had not God, etc., down to what true poverty does is added.
13.11: 13.11 Substance, etc. They that will become rich fall into temptation, etc., down to he will receive the manifold gifts of the beatitude above, of which:
13.12: 13.12 Hope that is deferred, etc. Because undoubtedly, etc., down to for he is the tree of life to those who lay hold on him.
13.13: 13.13 He that detracts. Otherwise, etc., down to whence: If a man be overtaken in any fault, etc.
13.14: 13.14 The law of the wise. From the time man begins to be wise, he uses this law, to avoid death and acquire life.
13.16: 13.16 With counsel, above all the divine, which is in the Scriptures. For he is a fool who lives outside this counsel, though he seem naturally prudent.
13.20: 13.20 He that walks with the wise. Any simple man or rustic, who cannot comprehend the secrets of wisdom, if nevertheless he follows by living the examples of the wise, will rightly be numbered among the wise. A friend of fools. He who loves fools, not because they are men, but for their folly, because they are mimes or actors or the like, not that he may correct them by instructing, but make them worse by favoring: though he seem wise, will be held to the condemnation of fools.
13.22: 13.22 A good man, etc., often the good die without children, etc., down to the kingdom of God is given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof.
13.23: 13.23 Much food. Another translator, etc., down to and to both senses what he adds agrees.
13.24: 13.24 He that spares the rod hates his son, etc. For a good father anxiously instructs his son, and a Catholic master his disciple, lest he turn aside to iniquity.
14.1: 14.1 A wise woman, etc. She will destroy by living ill, and at times by openly reigning, etc., down to of whom he openly adds:
14.3: 14.3 In the mouth of the fool. Because fools by idle talk afflict the humble whom they despise; but these by the doctrine of the wise fortify themselves lest they be deceived.
14.4: 14.4 Where no, etc. This cleaves to the former, etc., down to who feeds the widow of Sarepta by whom he is himself fed.
14.6: 14.6 The scorner seeks wisdom, etc. As Caiaphas, etc., down to because they seek perversely, they never at all find.
14.7: 14.7 Go against, etc. Therefore the scorner does not find the wisdom he seeks, etc., down to and strive to give effort to meditating on it.
14.10: 14.10 A stranger. That is a reprobate, etc., down to whence is added: The Lord of the wicked, etc. The wise man fears and declines. As it is the part of a fool to trust in his own alacrity, etc., down to or after death bravely endure punishments.
14.17: 14.17 The impatient, etc. Indeed the impatient man is reprehensible, etc., down to is reckoned among the reprobate.
14.19: 14.19 The evil shall fall down before the good. Seeing their torments, etc., down to to see their sufferings.
14.24: 14.24 The folly of fools. Imprudence, as it were improvidence, is so called.
14.25: 14.25 A faithful witness delivers souls. The Catholic is preached, who faithfully preaches and brings forth the testimonies of the Scriptures; the heretic lies. Brings forth lies. Another translation: A deceitful deceiver sets souls on fire with a lie. The shape-changer, that is the devil, who falsely presents as good the evils he suggests: and while he promises eternal goods, leads to torments.
14.26: 14.26 In the fear of the Lord. The fear of the Lord gives confidence of strength, etc., down to hoped in the Lord.
14.27: 14.27 The fear of the Lord. This is their hope, etc., down to whence, The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, Psalm 9.
14.30: 14.30 The life of the flesh. By the flesh the weak, by the bones the strong. If the innocence of the mind is kept, even the things that are weak without are sometime strengthened; whence he adds: Envy is the rottenness of the bones, because by the vice of spite those things perish before the eyes of God that seem strong in human eyes. For the bones to rot through envy is for every strong thing to perish.
15.1: 15.1 A mild answer breaks wrath. He who humbly receives the words of one rebuking is already nearing pardon of the guilt he has incurred. He who talks back to the reprover provokes the wrath of the judge against himself.
15.2: 15.2 Pours out folly. By perverting Scripture, by putting his own senses before authority; like foolish philosophers, as Porphyry and Julian, who poured out the streams of their folly against the doctors of the Church.
15.5: 15.5 The fool laughs. Every sinner is a fool, who, given to earthly acts, foresees nothing of the future: he laughs at discipline while he derogates from divine correction.
15.7: 15.7 The heart of fools is unlike. Either unlike itself, in various thoughts, and never remains the same. Against which it is said of Anna: And her countenance was no more changed into different things.
15.10: 15.10 Evil doctrine. He that shall break one of these least commandments, and shall so teach men, shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven. For such, however, if they are corrected, a return to pardon lies open: but if they receive not the rebukes, they shall altogether die.
15.15: 15.15 All the days. All the time of the people of God, etc., down to they are delighted as in a continual banquet.
15.17: 15.17 It is better to be called to herbs. For it is much more useful to keep the innocence of simple life with charity, etc., down to depart from me, you workers of iniquity.
15.19: 15.19 Of the slothful, who are loath to work justice, etc., down to but because this does not hinder the good, he adds: The way of the just is without offense. For the just, whatever adversity they find in their conversation, are not offended, because by the leap of eternal hope and inward contemplation they leap over adversities.
15.23: 15.23 A man rejoices. It is human to rejoice in a sentence as if prudently uttered. But the truly wise man diligently considers not only what he says, but also the opportuneness of place, and time, and of the person to whom he speaks.
15.24: 15.24 From the lowest hell, etc. The first hell is the blindness of the sinning soul, lacking the knowledge of the true light, of which: Let them go down alive into hell, Psalm 54.
15.25: 15.25 The widow of the Church, namely his bride, for whose life he deigned to die.
15.26: 15.26 Shall be established: in judgment, when he will render worthy rewards not only for deeds, but for all words.
15.30: 15.30 The light of the eyes rejoices the soul. Rightly it delights the human mind, etc., down to for so the work glows the more. The light of the eyes. Another translation: The eye seeing good things delights good hearts, namely, of the Lord in the land of the living, which, because it contemplates in the eye of the mind, deservedly delights the heart, though it be afflicted outwardly.
16.1: 16.1 It is the part of man to prepare the soul. How then is it man's to prepare the soul, and God's to govern the tongue? but it signifies the time of persecution, of which it is said, Take no thought how or what to speak: for it shall be given you in that hour what you shall speak, Matthew 10.
16.2: 16.2 All the ways. So the actions of all, both the good and the wicked, what they think in secret, he discerns with an exact balance, whence he adds.
16.3: 16.3 Reveal to the Lord. We reveal our works when we bring to mind in all we do him whom we know to be hidden from nothing, and ask his help: and then he directs not only works but thoughts.
16.4: 16.4 The Lord has made all things for himself, etc. The Lord had no cause of working but his will alone, namely to show his goodness to the rational creature, whom he would make forever blessed: but him who of his own accord forsook the good of his condition, that is the devil, with his followers, he condemned with just severity.
16.5: 16.5 Is an abomination. Whoever ascribes to himself the good that he does, even if he seems to work no evil with his hands, loses the innocence of heart, in which he has preferred himself to the giver of goods: and therefore the Lord abominates such a man, whom he sees ungrateful for his benefits.
16.7: 16.7 When the ways of a man please the Lord. So great is the holiness of divine religion, etc., down to but have been converted also to the truth of the faith.
16.8: 16.8 Better is a little with justice, etc. It is better to serve God devoutly in simple conversation than to abound in many virtues and despise the deeds of neighbors.
16.10: 16.10 Divination is in the lips of the king. What other king errs not in judgment, etc., down to who filled the mouths of his prophets. Weight and balance. The just stones are strong, etc., down to he distributes the measure of faith and graces.
16.13: 16.13 The will of kings, etc., that is, of the just. Many kings and prophets have desired to see what you have seen, and have not seen. For these both resist vices, and are thronged by the service of virtues as of attendants. For the kings of the earth often detest just lips, as Herod John.
16.14: 16.14 The messengers of death. The angels of Satan, heretics, etc., down to whom it chances to have offended by speaking foolishly. Shall appease. JEROME, on the death of Fabiola. David purged homicide and adultery by a famine of seven days.
16.15: 16.15 In the cheerfulness of the king's countenance is life. Whoever deserve to see the cheerful face of Christ, to these it will be given to live with him forever. The latter rain in Judea is still wont to come when the harvests are already ripe, etc., down to but is the watering of the Lord above.
16.22: 16.22 A fountain of life. Because that preacher truly opens to his hearers the ways of life, etc., down to the good things they say they despise with a foolish heart.
16.24: 16.24 Well-ordered words are a honeycomb, etc. Many through eloquence, etc., down to which proceed from the inward sweetness of the soul.
16.26: 16.26 The soul of him that labors, labors for himself, etc. It is clear literally, etc., down to because he must needs do the good things he says.
16.27: 16.27 A foolish man digs evil. This can be understood specially of the heretic, etc., down to whence James: The tongue inflames the wheel of our nativity, being set on fire by hell, James 3.
16.29: 16.29 A wicked man allures his friend, etc. This can be taken of the heretic and of every favorer of the wicked: for the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust man is blessed.
16.30: 16.30 He that thinks with closed eyes, etc. It is graver to accomplish evil than to do it, etc., down to that he may not see what retribution of his evils follows.
16.32: 16.32 The patient man is better than the strong, etc. The victory is less to storm cities, etc., down to and subdues by the humility of patience.
16.33: 16.33 Lots are cast into the lap. As lots are cast into the lap, etc., down to as from the lap of the divine judgment.
17.1: 17.1 Better is a morsel. It is better to do small good things with charity, without the knowledge of preaching, this is to be a dry morsel, than to shine the more by virtues with an admixture of discord.
17.6: 17.6 The crown of old men, etc. The old men, patriarchs, prophets, who are celebrated with divine praise by the children of their children, that is the successors of the apostles: and it is the glory of the preachers of the New Testament, who deserved to be sons of the ancient fathers.
17.8: 17.8 A most acceptable jewel. He who faithfully awaits future rewards, etc., down to understanding prudently, For to them that love God all things work together unto good, Romans 8.
17.12: 17.12 It is better to meet a bear, etc. It was easier for the holy teachers to meet the fury of the Gentiles, etc., down to and this often is easier than to recall a heretic to the right faith, or to bring back a Catholic acting wrongly to good work.
17.13: 17.13 He who. To let go water, etc., down to whence on the contrary: He who imposes silence on the fool calms angers.
17.16: 17.16 What does it profit. What does it profit the unbelieving people of the Jews, etc., down to when he has neglected to have the wisdom of pious action?
17.17: 17.17 At all times. He who truly loves God keeps his love at all times; nor does he forsake in the distress of suffering him whom he confessed in the tranquillity of peace.
17.18: 17.18 A foolish man will clap hands. He is a fool who, when he takes up his brother's soul to rule, boasts of his own deeds, and does not rather bestow upon him with humble compassion whatever helpful aid he can. A joyful mind. He who rejoices in the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit, etc., down to has lost the glory of love.
17.24: 17.24 In the face of the wise. In the face of Christ shone the wisdom of the Godhead, etc., down to they search with all intention.
17.26: 17.26 It is not good to do harm to the just. This can be taken of the judge himself and prince of ages who willed to be struck for our salvation, and of all the rulers of the Church, who have either been stripped of their means by the wicked or consumed by death itself.
18.1: 18.1 The wicked man, when he is come into the depth, etc. He who, wrapped in the long darkness of sins, once despairs of the light, from despair relaxes the reins of sinning for himself; but the reproach of future damnation he escapes by no means, whom no memory of the divine fear restrained.
18.4: 18.4 Deep water. Because the Lord and the apostles openly unlocked to the world the sacraments of both Testaments, of which he adds: And the overflowing torrent a fountain of wisdom. Deep water, that is, the words of the wise wash minds and water them, lest they remain deformed with the filth of sins or fail from dryness.
18.9: 18.9 He who is soft and loose. For he who does not strictly carry out the good begun, by the looseness of negligence imitates the hand of the destroyer.
18.11: 18.11 The substance of the rich is the city of his strength. Earthly substance, etc., down to as by an impregnable wall wards off all the snares of enemies.
18.13: 18.13 He who answers before he hears. He who desires to be a master before he learns does not avoid the harm of folly. He who hastens inordinately to judge the deeds of neighbors before he fully knows the cause of both, shows himself worthy of confusion.
18.14: 18.14 The spirit of a man bears up his infirmity. And the man himself, etc., down to sustains by strength of mind. But a spirit to anger. For the angry man often says what, when appeased, he regrets having said, and often does not know whether he said it: whose madness however is very easily borne and lulled by the modesty of the wise. The gift of a man. The gift of charity, etc., down to and make him willingly obey himself.
18.17: 18.17 The just is first. Everyone who is truly just, etc., down to rewards his humility with a worthy reward.
18.19: 18.19 A brother that is helped. When the people of the Jews and Gentiles, etc., down to defend from the assault of unbelievers.
18.23: 18.23 The poor will speak with supplications. The humble in spirit humbly adore the Lord, like the Publican: the proud boast of their merits, like the Pharisee.
18.24: 18.24 A lovable man. A converted Gentile is more loved by the Lord than a Jew persisting in unbelief, from whom he was born according to the flesh. It can be understood also of the apostles, born of Judea; because they would love more the believers from the Gentiles than the unbelievers of their own nation.
19.1: 19.1 Better is the poor man. Better is the simple hearer of the word of God, if what he understands in the Scriptures he advances by doing, than the learned man, if in what he has cautiously understood he twists his lips to preach heresy.
19.2: 19.2 Where there is no, etc. The knowledge of heavenly life is necessary to the human soul, etc., down to from the state of blessedness fell into the punishment of misery and mortality.
19.3: 19.3 Folly, etc. Fools, when they forsake the way of truth, etc., down to with a mad mind they reprehend the Lord himself as though he had laid unbearable burdens.
19.4: 19.4 Riches add friends. The riches of the heavenly kingdom, which are proclaimed to be given to the faithful through the holy teachers, win many friends both to those same preachers and to God, their giver. But from the prophets, because they promise nothing of sure beatitude, even those whom they have are separated, converted to the most certain promise of the Lord's faith.
19.5: 19.5 A false witness. He had rebuked him who followed only words, now he rebukes him who corrupts the words of the Lord's authority by ill interpretation. That many things are more often repeated is a confirmation, as Joseph says, because it is the word of God, and is the more swiftly fulfilled.
19.10: 19.10 Delights are not fitting for a fool. The delights of the Scriptures are not fitting for a heretic, because he knows not how to use them well, nor does it become him who is still a servant of sin to be preferred to the just in the government of the Church.
19.11: 19.11 The doctrine of a man. Ecclesiastical doctrine, etc., down to and rightly is added: And his glory is to pass over wrongs. For it is the part of a perfect teacher so to bear patiently the wickedness of others as to know how to guard himself patiently from the wicked. For neither does his own cleanness suffice without endurance, nor endurance without cleanness.
19.13: 19.13 The grief of a father. God in nature ever impassible, yet is said to grieve after our manner, when he sees men, whom he created to believe in him and praise him, serving the devil. Whence it repented him that he had made man on the earth, and touched with sorrow of heart within: I will destroy, he says, man whom I have created from the face of the earth, Genesis 6. A continual dripping. As roofs that drip receive rain indeed, etc., down to and mixed with filth returns to the hearers.
19.15: 19.15 Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. He is called slothful who keeps awake by knowing rightly, but grows torpid by doing nothing; but slothfulness casts into sleep, because the vigilance of right thinking is lost by degrees while work ceases. Rightly is it added: And the idle soul shall suffer hunger. For since it does not direct itself, by restraining itself, to higher things, neglected it spreads itself below through desires, and while it is not constrained by the vigor of subtle studies, it is wounded by the hunger of base cupidity, so that where it pretends not to be bound by discipline, there hungering it scatters itself through desires of pleasures.
19.18: 19.18 Chastise your son. If you see one subject to you err, correct him diligently; but if he refuse to be corrected, act so cautiously toward him that he find nothing in your words or works from which he may sin the more. With this agrees what follows:
19.19: 19.19 He that is impatient shall suffer loss, and when he has taken by violence. For if for the hardness of a contradicting brother you slip into the vice of impatience, etc., down to for when the violent man has taken away money, for this he will unwillingly give his soul.
19.22: 19.22 Better is the poor man. Than he who, saying himself worthy of the name of man by excellence of virtues, is deceived unaware, while by pride he has lost the good things he has done.
19.24: 19.24 The slothful hides his hand. No one is so slothful, etc., down to for to put the hand to the mouth is to make the work agree with the voice.
19.28: 19.28 Devours. As a hungry man food, he eagerly seeks to perpetrate iniquity.
20.4: 20.4 In summer. The kingdom of God is compared to summer, because now the clouds of our sorrow will pass away, and the days of life shall shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.
20.7: 20.7 He shall leave blessed children after him. Not literally, but those following his examples. Whence all the elect are children of Abraham, to whom not present but future blessedness is promised, whence, The king who sits.
20.8: 20.8 The king that sits on the throne of judgment. Even if in this life the elect suffer evils from the reprobate, etc., down to receives what is worthy of his deeds.
20.9: 20.9 Who can say. He does not say, who has, etc., down to they despise the neighbors' as cheap, he adds: Diverse weights. A diverse weight, etc., down to by what indications we ought to direct our judgment.
20.11: 20.11 By his studies he is understood. For whomever with virtues and modesty of continence, etc., down to as on the contrary: The friend of fools shall become like them.
20.12: 20.12 The Lord has made both. Let no one fit to preach despise a simple brother, etc., down to giving to each according to the measure of his gift.
20.14: 20.14 It is naught. He who desires to prepare eternal rewards in heaven, it is evil which in the present he must bear, so that when he departs from the world he may glory, plainly foreseeing that the sufferings of this time are not worthy, etc.
20.15: 20.15 There is gold and a multitude. This is the boast of the wise buyer, etc., down to and to be likened to precious vessels.
20.17: 20.17 The bread of lying is sweet to a man, etc. In whatever member one has sinned more, etc., down to which in superfluous words at feasting had flowed away.
20.21: 20.21 The inheritance. Those who through the wickedness of avarice desire to be multiplied in this life, etc., down to is an abomination before God.
20.23: 20.23 Diverse weight is an abomination before God, a deceitful balance, etc. He has a double weight and a deceitful balance in his heart, etc., down to or his soul consecrated to God in baptism.
20.25: 20.25 It is destruction to a man to devour the saints, and after vows to retract. If it is sin to harm anyone, etc., down to and those who, to fulfill their vows, persecute the saints, eternal damnation awaits. Therefore he adds:
20.26: 20.26 A wise king scatters the wicked, and bends a wheel over them. It was the custom of the ancients, etc., down to to which wheel is contrary the crown of life which God promises to those who love him.
20.30: 20.30 The blueness of a wound. For when we are struck outwardly, etc., down to because as the belly digests food, so the mind by turning over digests cares.
21.1: 21.1 As the divisions. Of all men, not only of the king, the heart is in the hand of the Lord, because in his hand are all the ends of the earth. But he calls king every saint who knows how to conquer in himself the wars of vices and to root out the shoots of malice. For as the Lord by the divisions of the waters fills the ends of the earth and of the air together, and covers also the upper parts of heaven with waters, so he inclines the heart of the king whithersoever he will, because as he distributes the divisions of graces according to his will both to angels and men; so he renders the hearts of the saints worthy of what gifts he will. And let the Pelagian be silent, because without the grace of God there is no place for salvation.
